summary: Defines a Node-Id sub-object for the Record Route Object. In MPLS traffic engineering Fast Reroute, the point of local repair needs the merge point address to select a backup tunnel, and existing mechanisms do not reliably provide it. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: If a road closes, drivers need to know where the detour rejoins the main road. This adds a small field so the routers learn that meeting point.

questions: what is the rro node-id flag 0x20
how does the plr find the merge point
why does fast reroute need the merge point address
subtitle: A new flag on Record Route entries lets a router find where a backup tunnel rejoins the protected path, even across areas and ASes.

tldr.problem: In MPLS TE Fast Reroute, the Point of Local Repair needs the Merge Point address to pick a backup tunnel, but Record Route entries may hold either node-ids or interface addresses, and across IGP areas or ASes the PLR cannot map one to the other.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4561 defines a new flag, 0x20, on the existing RRO IPv4 and IPv6 sub-objects. When set, the address is the node-id, so the PLR can compare node-ids from the primary and backup tunnels' RROs.
tldr.outcome: With node-ids marked, Fast Reroute can protect inter-domain TE LSPs against failure of an ABR or ASBR. The RFC introduces no new security issues.

facts.label: Carried in
facts.value: RRO IPv4 and IPv6 sub-objects in RSVP Resv messages

today: RFC 4561 is a Standards Track document published in June 2006. The metadata for this RFC lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Merge Point Problem
sections.content:
MPLS Fast Reroute (FRR) protects Traffic Engineering LSPs from link, node or Shared Risk Link Group failure. Backup tunnels are set up in advance, and when a resource fails, every protected LSP crossing it is moved onto the matching backup tunnel.

A backup tunnel starts at the Point of Local Repair (PLR) and ends at the Merge Point (MP), where it rejoins the protected path. When a fast reroutable LSP is first signaled, the PLR must dynamically pick a backup tunnel that meets the primary LSP at a downstream router, and that satisfies its bandwidth protection and link or node protection request.

One way to check the first condition is to look through the primary tunnel's Record Route Object (RRO) for the MP's address. The catch is that, per RFC 3209, RRO IPv4 and IPv6 sub-objects in Resv messages can carry node-ids, interface addresses, or both. In the RFC's example, router R2 may list different interface addresses in the RROs of the primary tunnel T1 and the backup tunnel B1.
sections.eli5: A router needs to know where its detour joins the main road. But the road signs name each door of a building instead of the building, so the router cannot tell two doors belong to the same building.

sections.title: Why Existing Mechanisms Fall Short
sections.content:
Inside a single IGP area the problem is easy. The PLR's IGP topology database lists every interface on the tail-end of the backup tunnel, so it can match any address in the RRO to the MP, whether that address is an interface address or a node-id.

That routing information is not available between domains, where a domain is an IGP area or an Autonomous System. The PLR cannot then be sure that a backup tunnel meets the protected LSP at the MP. As a result, as the abstract puts it, MPLS Fast Reroute cannot be used to protect inter-domain TE LSPs from failure of an Area Border Router (ABR) or Autonomous System Border Router (ASBR).

The RFC's Figure 1 shows the case: a protected LSP from R0 to R3 across areas 1, 0 and 2, with backup tunnel B1 from R1 to R2 following the R1-ABR3-R2 path to avoid ABR1. The PLR R1 must work out that T1 and B1 meet at R2.

The RFC applies to the Facility backup method of FRR, and the requirements for FRR on inter-domain LSPs come from RFC 4105 and RFC 4216.
sections.eli5: Inside one town, the router has a full map and can match doors to buildings. Between towns it has no map, so it needs the sign itself to say which building it is.

sections.title: The Node-Id Flag
sections.content:
RFC 3209 defines the IPv4 and IPv6 RRO sub-objects, and RFC 4090 adds two flags, Local Protection Available and Local Protection in Use. RFC 4561 adds a third flag, Node-id, with value 0x20.

When set, the address in the sub-object is a node-id: the 'Router Address' of RFC 3630 (OSPF-TE) or the 'Traffic Engineering Router ID' of RFC 3784 (IS-IS TE). A node MUST use the same address consistently, and once an address is used in the RRO sub-object it SHOULD be used for the whole lifetime of the TE LSP.

An IPv4 or IPv6 sub-object with this flag set is called a node-id sub-object. The fix is to insert one into the RRO carried in the RSVP Resv message. It is RECOMMENDED that an LSR that records a node-id address in an RRO sub-object also set the flag. The RFC notes the node-id sub-object may have other uses besides picking a backup tunnel.
sections.eli5: The new flag is a sticker on an address that says 'this is the router's own name, not one of its doors'. The router has to keep using the same name for as long as the path lives.

sections.title: Finding the Merge Point
sections.content:
An implementation may choose between two ways of filling the RRO in the Resv message. Either it adds the node-id sub-object and, when needed, a separate sub-object recording the interface address. Or it adds the interface-address sub-object and, when needed, a node-id sub-object. For an inter-domain fast reroutable LSP, the first approach yields a node-id sub-object and a label sub-object, plus an interface sub-object if one is required. The second yields an interface sub-object, a label sub-object and a node-id sub-object.

The PLR then has two cases. In Case 1, the backup tunnel's destination is the MP's node-id, and the PLR compares that destination address with the node-id in the primary tunnel's RRO. In Case 2, the backup tunnel ends at some other address, so a node-id sub-object MUST also appear in the backup tunnel's RRO, and the PLR compares the node-ids in the RROs of both tunnels.

If both IPv4 and IPv6 node-id sub-objects are present, the PLR may use either or both. For inter-AS use, the RFC assumes the MP's node-id in the downstream domain does not overlap with any node-id of an LSR in the PLR's own AS.
sections.eli5: Either the detour is already headed to the building, so the router just checks the name, or the detour ends at some other door and must also show the building's name so the two can be matched.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says this document does not introduce new security issues. The security considerations of RSVP (RFC 2205) and RSVP-TE (RFC 3209) remain relevant, since the node-id is carried in the same RRO those protocols already define.
sections.eli5: It only adds a label to something that already exists, so it does not add new ways to cheat. The old safety rules still apply.
